questions.stem: Which sequence should the nurse use to assess a client's abdomen?

opts.t: Inspect, auscultate, percuss, palpate
opts.r: Correct. Auscultation occurs before percussion and palpation because manipulation can alter bowel sounds.

opts.t: Inspect, palpate, percuss, auscultate
opts.r: Palpation before auscultation can change bowel activity and makes the finding less reliable.

opts.t: Auscultate, inspect, palpate, percuss
opts.r: Inspection is performed first to observe contour, scars, and distention before touching the abdomen.

opts.t: Palpate, percuss, auscultate, inspect
opts.r: This sequence alters findings before the baseline assessment is obtained.

questions.tip: Abdomen is the exception: I-A-P-P.

questions.stem: Which instruction should the nurse give a client who is collecting a clean-catch urine specimen?

opts.t: Collect the first urine that leaves the body in the sterile container.
opts.r: The initial stream may contain organisms from the urethra or skin and can contaminate the specimen.

opts.t: Cleanse the area, begin voiding, then collect urine midstream without touching the container interior.
opts.r: Correct. Midstream collection after cleansing reduces contamination while preserving a usable specimen.

opts.t: Save all urine for 24 hours in a sterile cup.
opts.r: A 24-hour specimen is a different collection procedure and requires a large container and specific storage instructions.

opts.t: Collect urine after taking an antibiotic dose.
opts.r: Antibiotics can affect culture results; collection timing follows the prescription and is often before treatment begins.

questions.tip: Clean catch: cleanse, start voiding, then catch the middle of the stream.

questions.stem: A client with a seizure disorder is admitted to the unit. Which intervention should the nurse include in the plan of care?

opts.t: Insert a tongue blade at the bedside for use during a seizure.
opts.r: Nothing is placed in the client's mouth during a seizure because it can cause injury or airway obstruction.

opts.t: Pad side rails and keep suction and oxygen equipment available.
opts.r: Correct. Padding reduces injury risk and ready access to suction and oxygen supports airway care if needed.

opts.t: Apply wrist restraints before the client sleeps.
opts.r: Restraints can injure a seizing client and are not a seizure-prevention intervention.

opts.t: Keep the bed elevated to allow rapid observation.
opts.r: The bed should be kept low to reduce fall injury risk.

questions.tip: Seizure safety: pad rails, bed low, suction and oxygen ready, and nothing in the mouth.

questions.stem: During tracheostomy suctioning, which finding indicates the nurse should stop suctioning and reoxygenate the client?

opts.t: The client coughs during catheter insertion.
opts.r: Coughing can occur with suctioning and is not by itself a reason to stop if the client remains stable.

opts.t: The oxygen saturation drops from 96% to 86%.
opts.r: Correct. A significant drop in oxygen saturation indicates hypoxemia. The nurse stops suctioning, provides oxygen, and reassesses.

opts.t: A small amount of thick secretion is removed.
opts.r: Removing secretions is the purpose of suctioning; secretion amount alone does not indicate intolerance.

opts.t: The client asks when suctioning will be finished.
opts.r: The nurse explains and provides comfort, but this does not signal physiologic intolerance.

questions.tip: Suction only as needed, limit each pass, and stop for hypoxemia or distress.

questions.stem: Which position is safest when the nurse provides oral care to an unconscious client?

opts.t: Supine with the head flat.
opts.r: A flat supine position increases aspiration risk from oral secretions or rinse fluid.

opts.t: Side-lying with the head turned to the side.
opts.r: Correct. Side-lying promotes drainage from the mouth and decreases aspiration risk.

opts.t: Trendelenburg with the feet elevated.
opts.r: Trendelenburg does not protect the airway and can worsen aspiration risk.

opts.t: High-Fowler with the chin lifted upward.
opts.r: An unconscious client may not maintain airway protection in this position; side-lying is safer for oral drainage.

questions.tip: For an unconscious client, turn to the side and use suction as needed during oral care.

questions.stem: A nurse needs to operate a fire extinguisher. Which action is part of the PASS method?

opts.t: Pull the pin before aiming at the base of the fire.
opts.r: Correct. PASS means Pull the pin, Aim at the base, Squeeze the handle, and Sweep side to side.

opts.t: Activate the alarm after extinguishing the fire.
opts.r: Alarm activation occurs immediately in the RACE sequence; it is not delayed until after extinguishing a fire.

opts.t: Spray the top of the flames first.
opts.r: The extinguisher is aimed at the base of the fire to remove the fuel source.

opts.t: Open all doors to clear smoke.
opts.r: Closing doors helps contain fire and smoke; opening doors can spread them.

questions.tip: RACE manages the event; PASS operates the extinguisher.

questions.stem: Which action is correct when performing passive range-of-motion exercises for a client with hemiplegia?

opts.t: Move each joint quickly through the full range until resistance is felt.
opts.r: Rapid movement and forcing against resistance can cause injury or pain.

opts.t: Support the limb above and below the joint and move it slowly until resistance or discomfort occurs.
opts.r: Correct. Supporting the limb and moving slowly protects the joint; movement stops at resistance or discomfort.

opts.t: Exercise only the unaffected side to prevent fatigue.
opts.r: The affected side needs gentle movement to maintain mobility and reduce contractures when prescribed.

opts.t: Hyperextend the joint briefly to increase flexibility.
opts.r: Hyperextension can damage tissue and is not part of safe range-of-motion exercise.

questions.tip: ROM is slow, smooth, supported, and never forced.

questions.stem: A client is 4 hours after abdominal surgery and needs to cough. Which instruction should the nurse provide?

opts.t: Avoid coughing because it can open the incision.
opts.r: Coughing and deep breathing help prevent postoperative pulmonary complications when performed safely.

opts.t: Splint the incision with a pillow while coughing.
opts.r: Correct. Splinting supports the incision, decreases discomfort, and allows the client to cough effectively.

opts.t: Hold the breath for 20 seconds before coughing.
opts.r: Prolonged breath holding is not required and can be uncomfortable or unsafe.

opts.t: Lie flat before coughing to relax the abdomen.
opts.r: An upright position promotes lung expansion and effective coughing better than lying flat.

questions.tip: After abdominal surgery: sit up, splint the incision, deep breathe, and cough.

questions.stem: Which instruction should the nurse give a client who is learning to ambulate with a walker?

opts.t: Move the weak leg forward before moving the walker.
opts.r: Moving the weak leg before the walker reduces stability.

opts.t: Move the walker forward, advance the weak leg, then advance the stronger leg.
opts.r: Correct. The walker provides support before the weaker leg moves, followed by the stronger leg.

opts.t: Carry the walker while taking several steps.
opts.r: Lifting and carrying the walker removes the stable base of support and increases fall risk.

opts.t: Keep the walker far ahead of the body to lengthen each step.
opts.r: The walker should remain within a safe reach; placing it too far ahead destabilizes the client.

questions.tip: With a walker: walker, weak leg, strong leg.

questions.stem: A client receives oxygen by simple face mask. Which flow rate should the nurse use to prevent rebreathing exhaled carbon dioxide?

opts.t: 1 L/min
opts.r: This flow is too low for a simple face mask and can allow carbon dioxide rebreathing.

opts.t: 3 L/min
opts.r: A simple mask requires at least 5 L/min to clear exhaled carbon dioxide.

opts.t: 5 L/min
opts.r: Correct. A simple face mask requires a minimum flow of 5 L/min; lower flows can cause carbon dioxide rebreathing.

opts.t: 15 L/min
opts.r: This may be used for a nonrebreather mask, but it is not the minimum requirement for a simple face mask.

questions.tip: Simple mask: never below 5 L/min.

questions.stem: A conscious adult suddenly cannot speak or cough after eating. Which action should the nurse take?

opts.t: Offer small sips of water.
opts.r: Fluids can worsen airway obstruction and delay emergency action.

opts.t: Deliver abdominal thrusts until the object is expelled or the client becomes unresponsive.
opts.r: Correct. A conscious adult with severe airway obstruction requires abdominal thrusts, with modifications for pregnancy or marked obesity.

opts.t: Perform a blind finger sweep.
opts.r: Blind sweeps can push an object deeper and cause injury.

opts.t: Begin chest compressions while the client is standing.
opts.r: Chest compressions begin after an unresponsive client is placed on a firm surface.

questions.tip: Severe choking: unable to speak, cough, or breathe = immediate abdominal thrusts for most conscious adults.

questions.stem: A nurse notes that a client's peripheral IV site is cool, pale, swollen, and painful. Which action should the nurse take first?

opts.t: Slow the infusion rate.
opts.r: Slowing an infiltrated infusion continues tissue exposure and is unsafe.

opts.t: Stop the infusion and remove the catheter according to policy.
opts.r: Correct. These are signs of infiltration. The infusion is stopped immediately and the site is managed according to the medication and policy.

opts.t: Apply a tourniquet above the site.
opts.r: A tourniquet does not treat infiltration and can worsen tissue injury.

opts.t: Flush the catheter with normal saline.
opts.r: Flushing can force additional fluid into tissue and must not be done when infiltration is suspected.

questions.tip: Infiltration is cool, pale, swollen, and slow. Stop the infusion first.

questions.stem: Which assessment finding is most consistent with phlebitis at a peripheral IV site?

opts.t: Coolness, pallor, and edema around the site.
opts.r: These findings are more consistent with infiltration.

opts.t: Redness, warmth, tenderness, and a palpable venous cord.
opts.r: Correct. Phlebitis produces inflammation along the vein, often with warmth, tenderness, erythema, and a palpable cord.

opts.t: A dry, intact dressing with brisk blood return.
opts.r: These are expected findings and do not indicate phlebitis.

opts.t: Clear fluid leaking from a disconnected cap.
opts.r: A leak indicates an equipment issue, not the inflammatory signs of phlebitis.

questions.tip: Phlebitis is red, warm, tender, and may feel like a cord; infiltration is cool and swollen.

questions.stem: Six hours after urinary catheter removal, a postoperative client has not voided and reports suprapubic pressure. Which action should the nurse take first?

opts.t: Insert an indwelling urinary catheter.
opts.r: Catheterization may be needed after assessment and an order, but it is not the first action when the client is stable.

opts.t: Assess for bladder distention and obtain a bladder scan if available.
opts.r: Correct. Suprapubic pressure and failure to void suggest retention. Assessment and bladder scanning guide the next intervention.

opts.t: Restrict oral fluids until the client voids.
opts.r: Fluid restriction can worsen the problem and is not a first-line action.

opts.t: Administer a diuretic.
opts.r: A diuretic is not a routine treatment for postoperative urinary retention and requires a prescription.

questions.tip: Postoperative no void plus suprapubic discomfort: assess and bladder scan before catheterizing.

questions.stem: Which finding should cause the nurse to suspect fecal impaction in an older adult?

opts.t: Large, formed stool once each day.
opts.r: A regular, formed stool pattern does not suggest impaction.

opts.t: Frequent small liquid stools with rectal pressure.
opts.r: Correct. Liquid stool can leak around an impaction, causing overflow diarrhea and rectal pressure.

opts.t: Increased appetite after meals.
opts.r: Increased appetite is not a typical sign of fecal impaction.

opts.t: Urine that is clear yellow.
opts.r: Urine appearance does not identify fecal impaction.

questions.tip: Overflow diarrhea can be a clue to impaction, especially with rectal pressure or a history of constipation.

questions.stem: A postoperative client coughs and the nurse sees the abdominal incision separate with loops of bowel visible. Which action should the nurse take first?

opts.t: Attempt to push the organs back into the abdomen.
opts.r: The nurse never attempts to reinsert eviscerated organs.

opts.t: Cover the area with sterile gauze moistened with normal saline.
opts.r: Correct. The nurse covers the organs with sterile saline-moistened dressings, positions the client to reduce tension, calls for immediate help, and keeps the client NPO.

opts.t: Apply a dry adhesive dressing tightly over the wound.
opts.r: A tight dry dressing can damage exposed tissue; sterile saline-moistened coverage is required.

opts.t: Place the client in high-Fowler position and ask for deep breaths.
opts.r: High-Fowler can increase abdominal tension; the client is generally positioned with knees bent to reduce strain.

questions.tip: Evisceration: cover with sterile saline-moistened gauze, knees bent, notify surgeon, NPO. Never push organs back.

questions.stem: A client dies in the hospital and is an organ donor. Which action should the nurse take?

opts.t: Remove all tubes and lines immediately before notifying the organ procurement organization.
opts.r: Lines and tubes may be needed for donor evaluation; the nurse follows the organ procurement organization's instructions before removing them.

opts.t: Follow facility policy and notify the appropriate organ procurement organization.
opts.r: Correct. Potential donors are referred according to policy. The procurement organization coordinates evaluation and family discussion, not the bedside nurse acting independently.

opts.t: Ask the family to sign donation consent before providing privacy.
opts.r: The nurse provides compassionate care and follows the designated referral process; donation discussions follow policy and trained personnel.

opts.t: Transport the body to the morgue before documenting death.
opts.r: Required pronouncement, documentation, identification, and policy steps occur before transport.

questions.tip: For potential organ donation, preserve lines and follow the organ procurement referral process.

questions.stem: A client newly diagnosed with cancer says, 'I am sure I am going to die.' Which response by the nurse is therapeutic?

opts.t: 'You should not think that way; many people survive cancer.'
opts.r: This offers false reassurance and shifts away from the client's expressed fear.

opts.t: 'Tell me more about what feels most frightening right now.'
opts.r: Correct. This open-ended response acknowledges the concern and invites the client to explore feelings.

opts.t: 'Your provider will explain the treatment plan later.'
opts.r: Deferring the concern does not address the client's immediate emotional need.

opts.t: 'You need to stay positive for your family.'
opts.r: This is judgmental and may prevent honest expression of fear.

questions.tip: Therapeutic communication explores feelings with open-ended questions instead of giving false reassurance.

questions.stem: Which nursing intervention best promotes sleep for a hospitalized client?

opts.t: Schedule routine vital signs, medications, and hygiene care at separate times overnight.
opts.r: Repeated interruptions fragment sleep and should be minimized when clinically safe.

opts.t: Cluster necessary nighttime care and reduce light and noise.
opts.r: Correct. Clustering care and controlling the environment reduce avoidable sleep disruption.

opts.t: Offer caffeinated tea with the evening snack.
opts.r: Caffeine can delay sleep and reduce sleep quality.

opts.t: Keep the television on at low volume throughout the night.
opts.r: Light and sound from a television can disturb sleep.

questions.tip: Promote sleep by clustering care, reducing noise and light, and protecting a quiet period.

questions.stem: Which action is appropriate when caring for a client at high risk for falls?

opts.t: Raise all four side rails whenever the client is in bed.
opts.r: Four raised rails can be considered a restraint and may increase injury if a client attempts to climb over them.

opts.t: Keep two side rails up as appropriate, place the bed low, and ensure the call light is reachable.
opts.r: Correct. These measures support safe mobility and access to assistance without unnecessary restriction.

opts.t: Apply a vest restraint whenever the client is alone.
opts.r: Restraints are a last resort after less restrictive measures fail and require orders and monitoring.

opts.t: Place the bedside table out of reach to discourage the client from getting up.
opts.r: Needed items should be reachable to reduce unsafe unassisted movement.

questions.tip: Fall prevention uses low bed, reachable call light, clear path, and least restrictive measures.

questions.stem: Before obtaining a capillary blood glucose value, which action should the nurse take?

opts.t: Use the side of the fingertip after allowing an alcohol-cleaned site to dry.
opts.r: Correct. The side of the fingertip is less painful, and allowing alcohol to dry prevents dilution of the sample and discomfort.

opts.t: Use the center of the thumb because it has the largest blood supply.
opts.r: The thumb and index finger are generally avoided because they are used frequently and can be more sensitive.

opts.t: Squeeze the finger firmly until a large drop forms.
opts.r: Excessive squeezing can dilute the sample with tissue fluid and affect accuracy.

opts.t: Puncture an edematous finger to obtain more blood.
opts.r: Edematous sites can produce inaccurate results and should be avoided.

questions.tip: Fingerstick: warm, clean, dry, use the side of the fingertip, and avoid excessive squeezing.

questions.stem: Which technique should the nurse use to assess for pitting edema in a client's lower leg?

opts.t: Palpate the popliteal pulse for 30 seconds.
opts.r: Pulse assessment evaluates arterial perfusion, not edema.

opts.t: Press a thumb over the tibia for several seconds and observe for an indentation.
opts.r: Correct. Sustained pressure over a bony area such as the tibia reveals pitting and allows grading after release.

opts.t: Tap the calf with a reflex hammer.
opts.r: A reflex hammer assesses neurologic reflexes, not edema.

opts.t: Measure oxygen saturation on the great toe.
opts.r: Oxygen saturation does not determine whether edema is pitting.

questions.tip: Assess pitting edema by pressing over a bony area, such as the tibia, then grading the remaining indentation.

questions.stem: Which client should the nurse question before applying a heating pad?

opts.t: A client with diabetic neuropathy and decreased sensation in the feet.
opts.r: Correct. Decreased sensation raises burn risk because the client may not perceive excessive heat.

opts.t: A client with a muscle strain 48 hours ago.
opts.r: Heat may be prescribed later in recovery to promote comfort and circulation, depending on the injury plan.

opts.t: A client who requests warmth before bedtime.
opts.r: Heat may be used safely when indicated if skin integrity and sensation are intact and it is monitored.

opts.t: A client with mild menstrual cramping.
opts.r: Heat is commonly used for comfort with cramping when no contraindication is present.

questions.tip: Never apply heat without checking skin integrity, circulation, and sensation; impaired sensation increases burn risk.

questions.stem: A client says, 'I am not worried about my procedure,' while wringing their hands and avoiding eye contact. Which action should the nurse take?

opts.t: Document that the client denies anxiety and leave the room.
opts.r: The client's nonverbal behavior conflicts with the statement and requires further assessment.

opts.t: Acknowledge the observed behavior and invite the client to talk about concerns.
opts.r: Correct. The nurse uses the discrepancy between verbal and nonverbal cues to explore possible anxiety without judgment.

opts.t: Tell the client to stop fidgeting because it makes others uncomfortable.
opts.r: This is judgmental and does not promote therapeutic communication.

opts.t: Assure the client that there is nothing to worry about.
opts.r: False reassurance dismisses the client's potential concerns.

questions.tip: When words and behavior conflict, explore the nonverbal cue rather than assuming the words are complete.

questions.stem: Before administering an oral medication, which action best verifies the client's identity?

opts.t: Ask the client to state their room number.
opts.r: Room number is not an approved client identifier and can change.

opts.t: Compare the medication administration record with the client's full name and date of birth on the identification band.
opts.r: Correct. Two approved identifiers, such as full name and date of birth, are compared with the medication record before administration.

opts.t: Ask a family member to confirm the client's identity.
opts.r: Family input may be helpful but does not replace use of approved identifiers.

opts.t: Match the client's diagnosis to the medication label.
opts.r: Diagnosis is not a reliable identity identifier and can lead to medication error.

questions.tip: Use two approved identifiers every time; room number and diagnosis do not count.

questions.stem: Which statement best demonstrates the Recommendation component of SBAR during a call to a provider?

opts.t: 'The client was admitted yesterday with pneumonia.'
opts.r: This is background information, not a recommendation.

opts.t: 'The temperature is 39.2 C and the blood pressure is 88/50 mm Hg.'
opts.r: This is assessment data, not a recommendation.

opts.t: 'I recommend you evaluate the client now and consider additional fluid resuscitation orders.'
opts.r: Correct. Recommendation states what the nurse is asking the provider to do next.

opts.t: 'The client has become more confused over the last hour.'
opts.r: This is part of the assessment or situation, not the recommended action.

questions.tip: SBAR Recommendation answers: What do I need from the provider now?

questions.stem: A client drinks 8 oz of juice and receives 250 mL of IV antibiotic solution. How much intake should the nurse document?

opts.t: 258 mL
opts.r: Eight ounces is approximately 240 mL, not 8 mL.

opts.t: 490 mL
opts.r: Correct. Eight ounces equals about 240 mL; 240 mL plus 250 mL equals 490 mL.

opts.t: 800 mL
opts.r: This incorrectly treats ounces as 100 mL each.
This amount does not reflect the volume conversion or the IV fluid amount.

questions.tip: For intake and output, 1 oz is approximately 30 mL.

questions.stem: Which finding is expected in the early postoperative period while a client is recovering from an abdominal surgery?

opts.t: Absent bowel sounds and no passage of flatus immediately after surgery.
opts.r: Correct. Temporary decreased bowel motility is common early after abdominal surgery; the nurse monitors for return of function and concerning symptoms.

opts.t: Persistent vomiting with progressive abdominal distention.
opts.r: These findings can indicate a complication and require prompt assessment.

opts.t: Rigid abdomen with severe increasing pain.
opts.r: Rigidity and escalating pain are not expected and may signal peritonitis or another complication.

opts.t: Large-volume watery diarrhea within the first hour.
opts.r: This is not an expected finding after abdominal surgery and requires assessment.

questions.tip: Early after abdominal surgery, bowel sounds and flatus may be absent; watch for worsening distention, pain, or vomiting.

questions.stem: A nurse finds a client seated on the floor beside the bed. Which action should the nurse take first?

opts.t: Assist the client immediately back into bed.
opts.r: Moving the client before assessment can worsen an undetected injury.

opts.t: Assess the client for injury and level of consciousness while calling for assistance.
opts.r: Correct. The nurse remains with the client, assesses for injury and neurologic status, then follows the safe-lift and reporting process.

opts.t: Complete an incident report before notifying the provider.
opts.r: Documentation and reporting occur after immediate client assessment and safety actions.

opts.t: Ask the client why they did not use the call light.
opts.r: The immediate priority is injury assessment, not assigning blame.

questions.tip: After a fall: stay with the client, assess first, get help, then notify and document per policy.

questions.stem: Which source is the most reliable indicator of a client's pain?

opts.t: The client's self-report of pain.
opts.r: Correct. Pain is subjective; when a client can communicate, self-report is the most reliable assessment source.

opts.t: The nurse's observation of facial expression.
opts.r: Behavioral cues can support assessment but do not override a communicating client's report.

opts.t: The client's heart rate and blood pressure.
opts.r: Vital signs can be affected by many factors and do not reliably quantify pain.

opts.t: The diagnosis listed in the medical record.
opts.r: A diagnosis does not determine the client's current pain experience.

questions.tip: Pain is whatever the experiencing person says it is; use self-report whenever possible.
